questions.title: What is the fundamental difference between a 'patch' in BLT and a 'token' in a standard LLM?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the core distinction the paper makes between patching and tokenization. The paper says BLT is 'tokenizer-free' and uses 'dynamically sized patches,' but a token is also just a group of bytes. Is the main difference simply that tokens come from a fixed vocabulary and patches don't? If so, why does the paper claim this leads to better efficiency?

questions.title: Why is BPE not considered an 'incremental patching' scheme?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.4, the authors define incremental patching as $f_p(\pmb{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\pmb{x})_{<i}$ and state that Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) does not satisfy this. I am confused because BPE is a deterministic algorithm. If I have a string and I know the first 10 bytes, shouldn't the BPE segmentation of those 10 bytes be fixed regardless of what the 11th byte is? Why does the paper claim the continuation sequence affects the tokenization of the prefix?

questions.title: How does 'dynamic patching' actually save FLOPs during inference?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that BLT improves inference efficiency by 'dynamically selecting long patches when data is predictable.' I understand that a larger patch means fewer steps for the Latent Transformer, but I don't see how the model 'knows' to choose a longer patch during inference. Does the model decide the patch boundary on the fly, and if so, how does that decision-making process itself not add significant computational overhead?

questions.title: How are the query and key/value roles swapped between the Encoder and Decoder cross-attention?
questions.question_body: I am looking at the architecture in Section 4. In the Local Encoder, the queries $Q_j$ correspond to the patches and the keys/values $K_i, V_i$ correspond to the bytes. In the Local Decoder, the text says the roles are 'interchanged.' Does this mean the queries $Q_i$ in the decoder are the bytes and the keys/values are the patches? If so, how does the decoder know which specific patch corresponds to which byte during the cross-attention step?

questions.title: In the FLOPs estimation equation, what does the variable $k$ represent?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to calculate the total FLOPs for a BLT model using the provided formula: $\text{FL}_{\text{BLT}} = \dots + \text{Cross Attn. FL}(h_{\mathcal{D}}, l_{\mathcal{D}}, m=k, r=k/n_p)$. The text defines $k$ as 'the ratio of patch-dimension to byte-dimension,' but then says $k=2$ in the figure. If $k$ is a ratio, why is it used as the context length $m$ in the $\text{Cross Attn. FL}$ function? I'm struggling to see how $k$ relates to the number of patches or bytes in the sequence.

questions.title: Does the 'scaling' of BLT imply that we can theoretically have an infinitely large model with a fixed inference budget?
questions.question_body: Section 5.3 says that BLT allows us to 'simultaneously increase model size and patch size while maintaining the same inference flop budget.' This is a very interesting claim. If we keep the inference FLOPs constant, but increase the patch size (reducing the number of steps), we can reallocate those saved FLOPs to make the Latent Transformer larger. Does this mean that token-based models have a hard ceiling on model size for a fixed inference cost, whereas BLT can theoretically scale model capacity indefinitely by just making the patches longer?

questions.title: How do the hash n-gram embeddings $E_n^{hash}$ help with 'orthographic knowledge'?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that BLT shows improvements in 'orthographic knowledge' (like spelling). I see that they use hash n-gram embeddings $e_i = x_i + \sum_{n=3,...,8}E_n^{hash}(\text{Hash}(g_{i,n}))$. Can you explain the intuition of why hashing 3-to-8 byte sequences into an embedding table specifically helps the model understand the spelling or internal structure of words better than just the raw byte embeddings $x_i$?
